guide.summary: Unit 2 covers the trans-Atlantic slave trade and the Middle Passage, how slavery was built into colonial and U.S. law, the experiences of enslaved people, the many forms of resistance from daily acts to revolts, free Black communities and abolitionism, and the path to emancipation.

sections.heading: The slave trade and the law of slavery
sections.body: Roughly 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships in the trans-Atlantic trade; most went to Brazil and the Caribbean, and a smaller share (around 400,000) to mainland North America. The Middle Passage was marked by crowding, disease, and high mortality, and captives resisted through revolts and refusing food. In 1619, about 20 Africans arrived at Point Comfort, Virginia. Colonies then wrote slavery into law: Virginia's 1662 law made a child's status follow the mother's (partus sequitur ventrem), making slavery hereditary and giving enslavers an incentive to exploit enslaved women; later slave codes restricted movement, literacy, and assembly. The Constitution protected slavery through the Three-Fifths Clause, the fugitive slave clause, and a 20-year delay before Congress could ban the international slave trade (banned in 1808). The cotton gin (1793) and cotton boom expanded slavery and drove a massive domestic slave trade that separated families.

sections.heading: Resistance
sections.body: Resistance ranged from everyday acts (slowing work, breaking tools, preserving African culture, religion, and family ties, secretly learning to read) to escape and revolt. Maroon communities of self-emancipated people formed in places like the Great Dismal Swamp and, on a large scale, Palmares in Brazil. Revolts include Stono (South Carolina, 1739), whose rebels headed toward Spanish Florida; Gabriel's planned revolt (Virginia, 1800); the German Coast Uprising (Louisiana, 1811); Denmark Vesey's alleged plot (Charleston, 1822); and Nat Turner's revolt (Virginia, 1831), after which states tightened slave codes. The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), led by figures including Toussaint Louverture, created the first Black republic and inspired enslaved people while terrifying enslavers. The Underground Railroad, a network of free Black and white allies, helped people escape; Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips and guided around 70 people to freedom.

sections.heading: Free Black communities and abolition
sections.body: Free Black Northerners built institutions: Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church (formally organized in 1816). Writers challenged slavery: Phillis Wheatley published poems in 1773; Olaudah Equiano's narrative (1789) described his capture and the Middle Passage; David Walker's Appeal (1829) urged resistance; Frederick Douglass's Narrative (1845) and his 1852 Fourth of July speech exposed American hypocrisy; Harriet Jacobs's Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861) revealed sexual exploitation of enslaved women; Sojourner Truth linked abolition and women's rights. Federal policy hardened: the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 forced Northerners to assist recapture, and Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) declared Black people could not be citizens. During the Civil War, enslaved people fled to Union lines, the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed people in Confederate areas and allowed Black enlistment (about 180,000 Black soldiers served, including the 54th Massachusetts), and the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery except as punishment for a crime.

sections.heading: Analyzing slave narratives and visual sources
sections.body: Slave narratives were often published with prefaces by white abolitionists vouching for their authenticity, which reveals both the authors' need to overcome doubt and the narratives' persuasive purpose. When analyzing images, such as the 1788 diagram of the slave ship Brookes, which abolitionists circulated to show the inhuman crowding of captives, identify the creator and purpose. Runaway advertisements, written by enslavers, nevertheless reveal the skills, appearance, and determination of people who escaped. Read these sources for evidence of agency as well as oppression.

sections.heading: Key terms and dates
sections.body: Important dates include 1619 (Point Comfort), 1662 (Virginia's law on hereditary slavery), 1739 (Stono), 1791–1804 (Haitian Revolution), 1808 (end of the legal U.S. international slave trade), 1831 (Nat Turner), 1850 (Fugitive Slave Act), 1857 (Dred Scott), 1863 (Emancipation Proclamation), and 1865 (Thirteenth Amendment). Terms include chattel slavery, maroon, manumission, the domestic slave trade, abolitionism, and self-emancipation. In free-response answers, use at least one specific person, text, or event per claim.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: When describing resistance, include both everyday acts and organized revolts, and explain how each challenged slavery.

keyTakeaways: Most enslaved Africans went to Brazil and the Caribbean, not North America.
Law made slavery hereditary and racial (Virginia 1662).
Resistance included daily acts, cultural survival, escape, and revolt.
The Haitian Revolution reshaped Atlantic politics.
Black writers and institutions drove abolition.
Emancipation came through war, self-emancipation, and the 13th Amendment.
commonMistakes: Defining resistance only as armed revolt.
Saying the Emancipation Proclamation freed all enslaved people.
Mixing up Nat Turner (1831) and Denmark Vesey (1822).
Assuming the North had no stake in slavery (textiles, shipping, banking).
examTips: When analyzing slave narratives, consider their audience (often Northern white readers) and purpose (persuading them to oppose slavery).
Connect revolts to the legal crackdowns that followed.
Use the 1662 Virginia law to discuss gender and slavery.

practice.prompt:
Evaluate the extent to which enslaved and free Black people resisted slavery through means other than armed revolt, 1739–1861.

Document 1 (summary): A 1739 colonial report on the Stono Rebellion describes enslaved people marching toward Spanish Florida after seizing weapons.

Document 2 (summary): The preface to Phillis Wheatley's Poems (1773) includes a statement from Boston leaders certifying that a young enslaved woman wrote the poems.

Document 3 (summary): David Walker's Appeal (1829) condemns slaveholding Christians and calls on Black people to resist enslavement and assert their humanity.

Document 4 (summary): In his Narrative (1845), Frederick Douglass describes how learning to read made him understand slavery and set him on the path to freedom.

Document 5 (summary): A runaway notice offers a reward for a man and woman who escaped together, noting that they may try to pass as free.

Document 6 (summary): Harriet Jacobs's Incidents (1861) describes hiding for nearly seven years in a tiny attic space to escape her enslaver and stay near her children.

Document 7 (summary): Accounts of Harriet Tubman describe her guiding dozens of people north on repeated trips through the Underground Railroad.

parts.label: Essay
parts.prompt: Write an argument responding to the prompt using at least four documents and outside evidence.

rubric.description: A defensible claim that establishes a line of reasoning about the extent of nonviolent resistance.
1 point for accurately describing three documents; 2 for using four documents to support the argument.
Specific evidence not in the documents (e.g., maroon communities, Nat Turner, the AME Church, Sojourner Truth, the Haitian Revolution).
1 point for explaining how evidence supports the claim; 2 for a complex argument (e.g., showing how forms of resistance overlapped or how revolts and legal crackdowns shaped other forms).
Explains how the perspective, purpose, context, or audience of at least two documents is relevant to the argument (e.g., Jacobs writing for Northern women; runaway notice written by an enslaver).

practice.sampleResponse:
Although armed revolts such as Stono drew the most attention, enslaved and free Black people resisted slavery primarily through escape, literacy, writing, and preserving family, forms of resistance that were less visible but more widespread and that steadily built the abolitionist movement.

Escape was the most common direct challenge. The runaway notice (Doc 5) shows a couple fleeing together; because it was written by an enslaver trying to recover 'property,' its worry that they might pass as free reveals how hard escape was to stop. Harriet Tubman's repeated trips (Doc 7) show that escape could become organized resistance, and Harriet Jacobs's seven years in hiding (Doc 6) show the extreme sacrifices people made. Jacobs wrote for Northern white women, so she stressed motherhood to win their sympathy.

Literacy and writing were also resistance. Douglass (Doc 4) describes reading as the path to freedom, which is why slave codes banned teaching enslaved people. Wheatley's poems (Doc 2) challenged claims about Black intellect, although the need for white men to certify her authorship shows the racism she faced. Walker's Appeal (Doc 3) went further, urging resistance; Southern states responded by banning its circulation.

Armed revolt still mattered. Stono (Doc 1) and Nat Turner's 1831 rebellion brought harsher laws, which pushed many toward escape and writing instead. Outside the documents, Black institutions such as the AME Church provided spiritual and organizational resources for abolition. These forms overlapped: Tubman escaped and then organized, and Douglass escaped and then wrote, showing that nonviolent resistance was the dominant and lasting strategy.
